props.title: Twentieth Century
props.initialSlug: Broadway producer pursues actress on luxury train

sections.content: Howard Hawks' screwball masterpiece Twentieth Century established core elements that defined the screwball comedy genre. John Barrymore's gloriously unhinged performance as theatrical impresario Oscar Jaffe and Carole Lombard's star-making turn as Lily Garland showcase the rapid-fire dialogue and battle-of-the-sexes dynamics that would influence films like His Girl Friday (1940) and Bringing Up Baby (1938). The confined setting of the Twentieth Century Limited train creates the perfect pressure cooker for their explosive chemistry, while Hawks' characteristic overlapping dialogue and physical comedy set new standards for pacing in comedy.

sections.content: The film's backstage theater setting and larger-than-life personalities influenced numerous subsequent Hollywood productions about show business, from All About Eve (1950) to The Producers (1967). Barrymore's Oscar Jaffe character, with his theatrical gestures and manipulative genius, became a template for depicting egomaniacal directors and producers. The train setting would be repeatedly borrowed by later screwball comedies like The Lady Eve (1941) and Some Like It Hot (1959), using the confined space to force antagonistic characters together. SUBHEAD: Impact on Screwball Comedy Genre

Twentieth Century helped establish several key conventions of screwball comedy: the transformation of a "normal" woman into an equally eccentric match for an already-bizarre male lead, the use of high society or show business settings, and rapid-fire dialogue delivered at near-manic pace. These elements would reach their apex in later films like The Awful Truth (1937) and His Girl Friday (1940), but Hawks' film showed how to balance sophisticated wit with broad physical comedy and genuine romantic chemistry.
